promptText: What is the central reframing this chapter proposes for how to think about writing a prompt?
options: A prompt conditions a probability distribution over next tokens -- you are shaping which continuations are likely, not issuing a command a deterministic executor obeys
A prompt is compiled into a fixed set of rules that the model executes deterministically, like a small program
A prompt only affects the model's output tone, never its factual content or structure
A prompt permanently updates the model's weights the same way a fine-tuning step would
explanation: Prompting as distribution-steering rather than instruction-giving is the idea that later explains why some prompting techniques work and others quietly backfire.

promptText: What distinguishes few-shot prompting from zero-shot prompting?
options: Few-shot includes one or more worked input/output examples so the model can infer the pattern by demonstration; zero-shot relies only on a natural-language task description
Few-shot requires fine-tuning a new model checkpoint on the examples before each request
Zero-shot always produces higher accuracy because it avoids diluting the context with examples
Few-shot means the prompt is shown to the model repeatedly in a loop until it converges on an answer
explanation: Few-shot is in-context learning in its most literal form and is often more reliable than a verbal description alone for tasks with a specific, hard-to-describe output shape.

promptText: Why does an instruction like 'only discuss our own product' tend to work more reliably than 'don't mention any competitors'?
options: The positive instruction defines a small, bounded region of acceptable output, while the negative instruction requires the model to correctly recognize and suppress an effectively unbounded set of ways a competitor could be referenced
Negative instructions are not supported by the tokenizer and are silently dropped from the prompt
Positive instructions are always shorter, and prompt length is the only factor that affects reliability
Models are explicitly trained to ignore any instruction phrased with the word 'don't'
explanation: A negative instruction requires the model to first consider the excluded thing in order to negate it, which can paradoxically increase its salience, whereas a positive instruction excludes everything else as a side effect.

promptText: What specific reliability problem does schema-constrained decoding (JSON mode) solve compared to a prompt instruction like 'respond only in JSON'?
options: It restricts token generation itself so that malformed syntax (stray text, wrong field names, invalid types) becomes structurally impossible, rather than merely asking the model nicely and hoping it complies
It guarantees that every field's value is factually correct, not just syntactically valid
It removes the need for any output parsing or validation code in the downstream application
It allows the model to skip the system prompt entirely and rely only on the schema
explanation: Constraining generation itself, rather than only asking nicely, makes malformed syntactic output effectively impossible -- but semantic correctness of the values is a separate, unsolved concern.

promptText: What is the difference between direct and indirect prompt injection?
options: Direct injection comes from the end user's own submitted input attempting to override instructions; indirect injection is embedded in third-party content the model consumes (a retrieved document, a web page, a tool result) that the user never typed
Direct injection only affects system prompts, while indirect injection only affects user prompts
Direct injection is a training-time attack, while indirect injection only occurs during fine-tuning
Indirect injection requires the attacker to have API access to the model provider's infrastructure
explanation: Indirect injection is generally more dangerous in agentic and RAG systems because the attack surface extends to every piece of external content the system touches, not just what the end user typed.

promptText: Why can't a system prompt be relied upon as a hard security boundary against a determined adversarial user?
options: The model's tendency to prioritize system instructions is a learned, statistical preference from instruction-tuning, not an architecturally enforced firewall -- system and user tokens are read through the same attention mechanism over the same sequence
System prompts are always visible in plaintext to any user who inspects network traffic, making them inherently insecure
Providers do not allow system prompts to contain any behavioral constraints, only persona descriptions
System prompts are capped at a handful of tokens, so they cannot contain enough content to enforce any real constraint
explanation: A sufficiently crafted adversarial prompt, especially combined with indirect injection, can still shift model behavior against the system prompt's intent, so security-sensitive constraints need enforcement outside the model entirely.

promptText: Mechanically, why does asking a model to 'think step by step' before answering improve accuracy on multi-step reasoning problems?
options: A Transformer performs a bounded amount of computation per generated token; writing intermediate steps turns each step into a new generation event that conditions on all prior steps, effectively giving the model more total forward-pass computation via its own output as scratch space
It triggers a special internal reasoning mode that runs a symbolic logic solver instead of the standard next-token prediction mechanism
It increases the model's context window size, allowing it to process the problem using more parameters
It lowers the effective sampling temperature during generation, making each subsequent token more deterministic
explanation: Chain-of-thought is not making the model 'think harder' mystically -- it gives a single-step-at-a-time predictor more forward passes to work with, made visible and available as context for later predictions.

promptText: In a few-shot prompt, why does putting three 'Positive' examples in a row before a genuinely ambiguous input risk biasing the model's answer?
options: Because generation is autoregressive and conditions on everything before it, a run of same-label examples can create a 'majority-label bias' that pushes the model toward repeating the recent label pattern regardless of the true input
Because the model can only process a maximum of two examples before discarding earlier ones from its context
Because same-label examples are automatically deduplicated by the tokenizer, leaving only ambiguous ones
Because few-shot examples are processed in a random order internally, so their order in the prompt has no effect on output
explanation: Models show measurable recency and primacy effects in few-shot examples, so example order should be randomized or balanced across labels rather than left as whatever order examples happened to be pulled in.

promptText: What is the key difference between using self-consistency and simply lowering the sampling temperature to get a more reliable answer?
options: Lowering temperature only sharpens a single reasoning path (and can make the model more confidently follow an early wrong step); self-consistency samples multiple independent reasoning paths at higher temperature and takes a majority vote, trading determinism for statistical robustness against any one path's error
They are functionally identical techniques that both eliminate randomness from generation entirely
Self-consistency requires access to raw logits, while temperature adjustment does not, so they apply to entirely different model architectures
Lowering temperature increases token cost roughly N-fold, while self-consistency has zero additional cost
explanation: The two address different failure modes: low temperature makes one pass more repeatable, while self-consistency makes the aggregate answer more correct by design through majority voting across genuinely different attempts.

promptText: Why might adding few-shot examples to a prompt sometimes hurt performance instead of helping?
options: The model cannot distinguish which aspects of an example are the intended pattern versus incidental -- if all examples share a coincidental trait (all short, all one tone), the model can overfit to that trait instead of the underlying task logic
Few-shot examples always exceed the model's maximum context window, causing a hard failure
Adding examples disables the model's instruction-following behavior entirely, reverting it to raw text completion
Few-shot examples are ignored by the model unless chain-of-thought prompting is also used in the same prompt
explanation: This is closely related to spurious correlation in classical machine learning; the fix is deliberately varying every dimension across examples except the one you're actually trying to teach.

promptText: Given the 'lost in the middle' effect, how should a long prompt containing several retrieved documents and key task instructions be structured?
options: Place the most relevant passages and the most critical instructions near the beginning or end of the context, and consider reinforcing critical constraints again near the end, since information buried in the middle of a long context is used less reliably
Always place the most important information exactly in the middle, since models are trained to prioritize the median position of any input sequence
It doesn't matter where information is placed, since attention mechanisms weight all token positions in a context equally by design
Split every document into single-token chunks so the model cannot lose track of any individual fact
explanation: This is a direct design implication of the model's positional weighting behavior, not a stylistic preference, and directly motivates context-ordering strategies in retrieval pipelines.

promptText: Why are delimiter-based defenses (wrapping untrusted content in tags like <untrusted>...</untrusted>) against prompt injection not considered fully robust?
options: The model's respect for delimiters is a learned, probabilistic tendency from training, not a hard parser-enforced boundary -- a sufficiently crafted injection can mimic a closing tag or otherwise shift behavior despite the delimiter's presence
Delimiters are stripped out by the tokenizer before the model ever sees them, so they provide no protection at all
Delimiters only work for XML-based content and have no effect on plain text or Markdown-formatted injections
Providers explicitly disable delimiter recognition for any prompt exceeding 500 tokens
explanation: Ultimately the model is still just predicting the statistically most likely continuation of the full token sequence it sees, delimiters included, which is why defense in depth outside the model is required.

promptText: A prompt that worked reliably for months suddenly produces inconsistent output, but the team hasn't changed the prompt text. What is the most likely first thing to check, and why?
options: Whether the underlying model itself was silently updated behind the same version alias -- many providers periodically update or auto-migrate models behind an unpinned identifier, which is the single most common cause of unexplained behavior drift with no code change
Whether the prompt template file has correct UTF-8 encoding, since encoding errors are the only cause of nondeterministic output
Whether the user's browser cache is serving a stale version of the chat UI, which is unrelated to the API call itself
Whether the vector database's disk has run out of space, since this is the only infrastructure factor that affects prompt behavior
explanation: Because different model checkpoints are trained differently, pinning to an explicit immutable model version and treating any upgrade as a deliberate migration event is the standard defense against this exact failure mode.

promptText: A team lets an automatic prompt-optimization framework (DSPy-style) search prompt phrasings against an evaluation metric with no human review. What is the main risk, and why?
options: The optimizer will exploit any gap between the stated metric and true intent -- e.g., converging on terse, format-matching but semantically wrong answers if the metric only checks exact-string match -- a direct analogue of reward hacking, and it may also overfit to the specific evaluation set's quirks
The optimizer cannot run without first fine-tuning the underlying model's weights, so this risk does not apply to prompt-only optimization
There is no risk, since any metric improvement mathematically guarantees a corresponding improvement in real-world output quality
The optimizer will only ever remove few-shot examples, never modify instructional text, limiting its potential for harm
explanation: An automated optimizer optimizes exactly what you measure; a narrow or biased evaluation set will produce a prompt that games the metric rather than genuinely improving quality, which is why human review of what changed remains necessary.

promptText: A ReAct-style agent interleaves reasoning with tool calls and their observations. Why does this pattern introduce injection risk beyond what plain chain-of-thought has, and what production safeguard follows from that mechanism?
options: Each observation returned from an external system becomes part of the model's context and can influence subsequent thoughts and actions exactly like any other prompt content, so a malicious or manipulated observation (e.g., a poisoned search result) becomes a new injection vector requiring the same untrusted-content delimiting, validation, and bounded iteration/action allow-listing as any other external content
ReAct agents execute all actions in a separate, fully sandboxed model with no shared context, so injection risk is actually lower than plain chain-of-thought
Observations are mathematically guaranteed to be truthful because they come from deterministic tool calls rather than model generation
The risk is purely theoretical since ReAct-style prompting has been fully deprecated in favor of single-shot prompting in production systems
explanation: An early bad or misleading observation compounds through subsequent reasoning the same way drift compounds in plain chain-of-thought, except the drift can now originate from a real external system, which is why bounded iteration counts and action validation are required.
